question_text: Find the equation of the circle passing through the points A(1,2), B(3,−4), C(5,−6).

insider_note: The two distance equations are only the setup — the marks sit in the centre, the radius and the final expanded form, so always finish at x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 rather than stopping at the centre-radius form.

steps.label: First equation from SA = SB
steps.margin_note: One mark for reaching a clean linear equation in x₁ and y₁. The squared terms must cancel; if they do not, an expansion is wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Three points, three equal distances. Two equalities are enough — SA = SB and SA = SC.
lines: Let S(x₁, y₁) be the centre of the circle.
S is the same distance from all three points.
steps.why: The centre of a circle is the one point at equal distance from every point on it. Squaring both sides removes the square roots, and the x₁² and y₁² terms are the same on both sides, so they cancel and leave a straight line.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to square both sides and trying to work with square roots.
Sign slip on (y₁ + 4)², which expands with +8y₁.
Dividing 4x₁ − 12y₁ − 20 = 0 by 4 but leaving the 20 as 20.

steps.label: Second equation from SA = SC
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Use A again, not B — reusing the same first point keeps the algebra short and the sign pattern the same.
steps.memory_tip: Keep A fixed in both equations. Then only the second point changes each time.
steps.why: A second equal-distance condition gives a second straight line. Two straight lines meet at one point, and that point is the centre.
common_mistakes: Using SB = SC here, which gives a correct but different pair and more arithmetic.

steps.label: Solve for the centre
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Subtracting is faster than substitution here because the x₁ coefficients are already equal.
steps.memory_tip: Both equations start with x₁, so subtract them and x₁ disappears in one line.
steps.why: Equations (1) and (2) both have coefficient 1 on x₁, so one subtraction removes x₁ and gives y₁ at once. Back-substitution then gives x₁.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order and getting y₁ = −2.
Putting y₁ = 2 into equation (2) and then mixing the two results.

steps.label: Find the radius
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work with r², not r — the equation of the circle needs r² anyway, so the square root is never taken.
steps.memory_tip: Any one of the three given points serves as the radius end. A is the shortest to compute.
lines: A = (1, 2) lies on the circle, so r = SA.
steps.why: The radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle, and all three given points are on it. Keeping r² avoids an unnecessary square root.
common_mistakes: Taking the square root to get r = 10 and then squaring it again later.
Using a point that is not on the circle, such as the origin.

steps.label: Equation of the circle
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Finish in the expanded general form; the centre-radius form alone is usually marked short.
steps.memory_tip: Centre (h, k), radius r gives (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Expand, then collect.
lines: Circle with centre (11, 2) and r² = 100 is
steps.why: The centre-radius form is the definition written down. Expanding it gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, in which g = −11, f = −2 and c = 25, and that is the form the rest of the chapter uses.
common_mistakes: Writing −22x as +22x because the centre x-coordinate is +11.
